Quality regressionJudge scores, thumbs-down, escalations, regenerate rateCorrelate with versions on traces (prompt, model snapshot, index, retrieval config); roll back the flag; add the failing cases to the regression set
Runaway agent costPer-run token burn, steps, tenant spend vs baselineHard budgets enforced in the gateway kill the run; loop detection; per-tenant caps; post-mortem on why the agent looped
Prompt-injection attack or abuseGuardrail trigger spikes, unusual tool-call patterns, data-egress attemptsBlock the source, disable the affected tool, review traces, add attacks to red-team evals
Cache breakagePrompt cache hit rate collapses, TTFT and cost jumpFind the change that altered the prefix (timestamp in system prompt, reordered tools) and restore prefix stability
Data leak reportUser report, privacy eval, auditTrace back to retrieval and cache keys; purge affected caches and indexes; fix scoping; notify per policy

PII, retention and access

LLM traces are full of user content: support conversations, documents, code. Treat the trace store as a production database of sensitive data.

  • Redact at the collector (emails, phone numbers, card numbers, secrets) before data leaves the service boundary; keep a reversible token vault only if a workflow truly needs re-identification.
  • Tiered retention: metadata and metrics for months; full payloads for days or weeks unless the customer opts in for longer; honor deletion requests across traces, eval datasets and fine-tuning sets.
  • Access control and audit for anyone reading payloads; enterprise customers will ask, and some will require zero retention of content.
  • Consent before using production traces in eval sets or training data, per your terms and the customer's contract.

Closing the loop

Observability is the input to improvement. A healthy loop looks like: alerts and sampled judging surface bad traces, someone triages and labels the failure mode, the case lands in the golden dataset, a fix is developed against it, the fix passes the gate, and the canary confirms it in production. Track the loop itself: time from a failure report to a regression test, and the share of eval cases that came from production.

Tooling landscape

CategoryExamples
LLM-native tracing + evalsLangfuse (open source), LangSmith, Arize Phoenix (open source), Braintrust, W&B Weave
Proxy / gateway-based loggingHelicone, Portkey, LiteLLM proxy, cloud AI gateways: capture usage and cost by sitting in the request path
General APM with LLM featuresDatadog LLM Observability, Grafana, New Relic, Honeycomb: useful when you want LLM spans next to the rest of your stack
InstrumentationOpenTelemetry SDKs, OpenLLMetry, OpenInference
Product analyticsFeedback and outcome events (accepts, edits, escalations) in your analytics stack, joined to trace ids

In an interview, name the categories and one example, and spend your time on what you'd record and alert on.

Observability in System Design Interviews

When to bring it up

  • When you finish the high-level design: "Every step emits a span with versions and token counts, so we can debug any bad answer end to end."
  • When cost comes up: "The gateway attributes cost per tenant and feature, and enforces budgets."
  • When the interviewer asks how you'd ship changes or handle a provider outage, or "how would you know if quality dropped?"

How to introduce it

  1. Tracing: one trace per request, spans for retrieval, model and tool calls, with prompt and model versions and token counts.
  2. Metrics and alerts: TTFT/TPOT, errors and fallbacks, cost per unit of value, cache hit rate, guardrail rates, sampled quality scores.
  3. Release process: versioned prompt and model bundles, offline gate, shadow, canary, flag-based rollback.
  4. Data handling: redaction, retention tiers, access audit.
  5. Loop: bad traces become eval cases.

Common deep-dive questions

"Support tickets say answers got worse yesterday, but there were no errors. What do you do?"

Bad Solution
Read some logs and tweak the prompt

Challenges: no way to localize the cause or confirm the fix; the tweak may break other cases.

Good Solution
Check recent deploys and roll back

Approach: look for prompt or code changes in the window and revert them.

Challenges: misses causes outside your deploys: provider model updates, stale indexes, new traffic patterns.

Great Solution
Slice quality by every versioned dimension, then fix and gate

Approach: plot sampled judge scores and implicit feedback by prompt version, model snapshot, index version, tenant and query cluster to localize the change; inspect low-scoring traces (retrieved chunks, tool results); roll back the responsible flag; add the failing traces to the golden set; ship the real fix through the gate and canary.

Challenges: requires versions on every span and online quality scoring, which is why you build them up front.

"How do you stop one agent run from spending $500?"

Budgets enforced outside the model (in the gateway or orchestrator): max steps, tokens and wall-clock per run, per-tenant daily caps, loop detection on repeated tool calls, real-time spend metrics per run with alerts, and a kill switch.

"What would you put on the on-call dashboard?"

TTFT and TPOT percentiles, error and fallback rates per provider, tokens per second vs rate limits, cost burn vs budget, prompt cache hit rate, guardrail and refusal rates, sampled quality score, and agent budget hits, each sliceable by tenant, feature and version.

Summary

  • Trace every request end to end with versions, tokens, retrieval results and tool calls; use OpenTelemetry, knowing the GenAI conventions are still evolving.
  • Monitor quality and cost as first-class signals alongside latency and errors.
  • Attribute cost per tenant, feature and outcome; enforce budgets in the gateway.
  • Version prompt, model and retrieval config as one bundle; roll out via shadow and canary with flag-based rollback.
  • Redact, tier retention and audit access: traces are sensitive data.
  • Close the loop: production failures become eval cases (see Evaluation), and the gateway that emits much of this telemetry is covered in Gateways, Routing & Reliability.

LLM System Design · Core Concepts

Fine-tuning & Adaptation

When to change a model's weights instead of its prompt, how SFT, LoRA, preference tuning and distillation work, what the data and training infrastructure look like, and how to serve and roll out many fine-tuned variants safely.

"Should we fine-tune?" comes up in almost every applied LLM interview, usually as a trap. Candidates who jump to fine-tuning for a knowledge problem, or who can't say what data they'd train on and how they'd know it worked, lose points. Candidates who climb a ladder of cheaper options first, then fine-tune for a specific measurable reason with a real data and eval plan, do well.

This page covers the decision, the main techniques at the depth an engineer needs, the data pipeline, training memory math, multi-adapter serving, and rollout. It assumes the summary table in the Fast Track.

The adaptation ladder

RungChangesGood forNot for
PromptingInstructionsEverything, firstBehavior the model can't follow reliably however you phrase it
Few-shot / examplesDemonstrations in contextFormat, tone, edge casesHundreds of examples (context cost every call)
RAGWhat the model seesPrivate, fresh, large or permissioned knowledge; citationsStyle, format, reasoning skill
SFT (often LoRA)Weights, via input→output examplesConsistent behavior: format, tone, domain jargon, tool-call schemas; making a small model do one task well; latency and costFacts that change; tasks without good examples
Preference / RL tuningWeights, via comparisons or rewardsSubjective quality (helpfulness, style), or tasks with automatic checks (code passes tests, math is correct)Teams without solid evals and reward signals
Continued pre-trainingWeights, via large unlabeled corporaNew languages, very specialized domains with billions of tokensAlmost every product team

Retrieval for knowledge, fine-tuning for behavior. Fine-tuning is a poor way to teach facts: the model memorizes them unreliably, can't cite them, and goes stale. It's an excellent way to make behavior consistent and to make a small, cheap model do one job as well as a big one.

Valid reasons to fine-tune, in interview language:

  • Cost and latency: "We classify 50M tickets a month; a fine-tuned 8B model matches the frontier model's accuracy on our eval at a small fraction of the cost and a quarter of the latency."
  • Consistency: "The prompt has grown to 6K tokens of rules and examples and still fails 8% of format checks."
  • Capability on a narrow task that prompting can't reach: domain-specific extraction, a proprietary DSL, a tool schema the model keeps getting wrong.
  • Deployment constraints: on-device or air-gapped deployment needs a small open model that must be specialized to be good enough.

Supervised fine-tuning (SFT)

SFT continues training on (input, desired output) pairs with the usual next-token loss, usually computed only on the output tokens. It's the workhorse: instruction tuning, format adherence, style, tool use, and distillation are all SFT underneath.

  • Data size: quality beats quantity. Behavior and format changes often need a few hundred to a few thousand carefully curated examples; the LIMA study got strong instruction following from 1,000 curated examples (Zhou et al., 2023). Narrow classification or extraction tasks benefit from thousands to tens of thousands.
  • Format: use the model's chat template exactly as it will be used in production, including the system prompt and tool definitions. Training-serving skew in templates is a common silent bug.
  • Hyperparameters to name: learning rate (full fine-tune ~1e-5; LoRA ~1e-4 to 2e-4), 1–3 epochs, sequence packing for efficiency, early stopping on validation loss and task metrics.
  • Overfitting signals: validation loss rising, outputs copying training phrasing verbatim, regression on general benchmarks.

Parameter-efficient fine-tuning (LoRA and friends)

Full fine-tuning updates every weight, which needs a lot of memory and produces a full model copy per variant. LoRA freezes the base weights and learns a low-rank update for selected matrices (Hu et al., 2021):

W' = W + (α / r) · B · A        W: d × k (frozen)   B: d × r   A: r × k
trainable parameters per matrix = r × (d + k)

Worked example, Llama 3 8B (hidden size 4,096, MLP size 14,336, 8 KV heads × 128 = 1,024-dim K and V), rank r = 16 on all seven linear layers in each of 32 blocks:

q_proj, o_proj   4,096 × 4,096   → 16 × 8,192  = 131,072 each
k_proj, v_proj   4,096 × 1,024   → 16 × 5,120  =  81,920 each
gate, up, down   4,096 × 14,336  → 16 × 18,432 = 294,912 each
per block = 2×131,072 + 2×81,920 + 3×294,912 = 1,310,720
× 32 blocks ≈ 42M trainable parameters (~0.5% of 8B) → ~84 MB adapter in BF16
same rank on q_proj and v_proj only ≈ 6.8M parameters
  • Rank and targets: r = 8–64 is typical. Targeting all linear layers usually beats attention-only at the same parameter budget.
  • Merge or keep separate: merge B·A into W for zero inference overhead, or keep adapters separate so one base model serves many variants (below).
  • Trade-off: LoRA can underperform full fine-tuning on large knowledge-heavy changes, but it also tends to forget less of the base model's abilities (Biderman et al., "LoRA Learns Less and Forgets Less", 2024). For most product tasks it is the right default.
  • QLoRA stores the frozen base in 4-bit (NF4) and trains LoRA adapters on top, making it possible to fine-tune a 65B model on a single 48 GB GPU (Dettmers et al., 2023).
  • Other PEFT methods (prefix tuning, prompt tuning, IA³, DoRA) exist; LoRA and QLoRA are what you'll see in practice and are enough to name.

Preference and reinforcement tuning

SFT teaches "produce this output." Preference and RL methods teach "produce outputs that score better," which suits goals that are easier to judge than to demonstrate.

MethodSignalHow it worksPractical notes
RLHF with PPOHuman preference pairsTrain a reward model on comparisons, then optimize the policy against it with PPO and a KL penalty to stay near the SFT model (Ouyang et al., InstructGPT, 2022)Powerful but complex: four models in memory, unstable, reward hacking
DPOPreference pairs (chosen, rejected)A closed-form loss that raises the likelihood of chosen over rejected relative to a frozen reference; no reward model, no RL loop (Rafailov et al., 2023)The practical default for product teams; variants relax its requirements: KTO learns from unpaired thumbs up/down, ORPO and SimPO drop the reference model
RL with verifiable rewards (e.g. GRPO)Programmatic checks: tests pass, answer matches, schema validatesSample several outputs per prompt, score them, push probability toward above-average ones; GRPO uses the group's mean score as the baseline instead of a value model (Shao et al., DeepSeekMath, 2024); used at scale for reasoning models (DeepSeek-R1, 2025)Excellent when you can grade automatically; watch for reward hacking (passing tests by special-casing them)
Hosted "reinforcement fine-tuning"Your grader functionProvider runs the RL loop on their model with your prompts and graderLets product teams use RL without RL infrastructure

Where preference pairs come from in a product: thumbs up/down, users choosing between two drafts, edits (the edited version is "chosen," the original "rejected"), expert reviewers, or an LLM judge calibrated against humans (see Evaluation).

Distillation: big model to small model

The most common fine-tuning project in industry: a large model does the task well but is too slow or expensive at volume, so you train a small model to imitate it.

  1. Collect real inputs from production (with consent and PII handling) or generate realistic synthetic ones.
  2. Generate teacher outputs with the large model, using your best prompt, possibly with reasoning, retrieval and self-checks that would be too slow at serving time.
  3. Filter: keep outputs that pass validators, tests or a judge; drop low-confidence ones; balance classes and edge cases.
  4. SFT the student (often with LoRA); if you control both models, you can also train on the teacher's token probabilities (logit distillation) for a richer signal.
  5. Evaluate head to head on a held-out set labeled by humans, not by the teacher, so you measure real quality rather than imitation.
  6. Route: serve the student by default and escalate uncertain cases to the teacher (a cascade).

Check the teacher's terms of service before training on its outputs; several providers restrict using outputs to build competing models. Distilling your own or open-weight models avoids the issue.

Fine-tuning retrieval models

Often the highest-leverage fine-tune in a RAG system isn't the LLM at all.

  • Embedding models: train contrastively on (query, relevant passage) pairs with in-batch negatives and hard negatives mined from your current retriever (passages that look similar but are wrong). Generate synthetic queries per chunk with an LLM when you lack real ones. Gains on domain jargon and internal acronyms can be large.
  • Cost to remember: a new embedding model means re-embedding the entire corpus and rebuilding the index (see the 50M-document estimate), plus a dual-index migration.
  • Rerankers: fine-tuning a cross-encoder reranker on (query, passage, label) improves precision without re-indexing, so it's often the cheaper first move.
  • Measure with retrieval metrics (recall@k, nDCG) on a frozen labeled set before and after (see RAG in Depth).

The data pipeline

  • Collection: production logs (with user consent and retention policies), expert-written examples, and teacher-generated synthetic data. Log the inputs and the context the model saw, or you can't reproduce examples.
  • Labeling: written guidelines, multiple annotators on a sample to measure agreement, adjudication of disagreements. Low agreement means the task is ambiguous, and no model will fix that.
  • Cleaning: exact and near-duplicate removal (hashing, MinHash), PII detection and scrubbing, toxic or low-quality filtering, license checks.
  • Splitting: a frozen eval set the training pipeline never touches, split by user or document (not by row) to avoid leakage; check n-gram overlap between training data and eval to catch contamination.
  • Coverage: include hard and adversarial cases, refusals the model should still make, and negative examples (inputs where the right answer is "none" or "escalate").
  • Lineage: version datasets with content hashes so every model can be traced to the exact data it saw, and so you can honor deletion requests.

Training infrastructure basics

full fine-tune, mixed precision with Adam ≈ 16 bytes per parameter (before activations)
  2 (BF16 weights) + 2 (BF16 grads) + 4 (FP32 master weights) + 8 (Adam m and v)

7B  → ~112 GB   → a multi-GPU node with sharding
70B → ~1.1 TB   → multiple nodes with FSDP / ZeRO-3
LoRA on 8B:   16 GB frozen base + adapter states (~42M × 16 B ≈ 0.7 GB) + activations → one GPU
QLoRA on 70B: ~35–40 GB 4-bit base + adapters + activations → one 80 GB GPU
  • Sharding: ZeRO stage 1/2/3 (Rajbhandari et al., 2019) and PyTorch FSDP shard optimizer states, gradients and finally parameters across GPUs, trading communication for memory.
  • Activation memory: grows with batch × sequence length; gradient checkpointing recomputes activations to save memory at ~30% extra compute.
  • Tooling: Hugging Face TRL and PEFT, Axolotl, Unsloth, torchtune for open models; hosted fine-tuning from model providers and clouds for closed models (supported models and methods change often, so check each provider's docs).
  • Compute cost: training FLOPs ≈ 6 × params × training tokens. A LoRA run on 8B with 20M tokens is at most 6 × 8e9 × 2e7 ≈ 1e18 FLOPs (LoRA skips weight gradients for the frozen layers, so closer to ~4×), about an hour on one H100 at ~30% utilization. Fine-tuning compute is rarely the expensive part; data and evals are.

Serving fine-tuned models

One merged model per variant

Simple and fastest per request, but each variant needs its own GPUs. Fine for one or two variants; wasteful for per-customer models.

Multi-LoRA serving

Keep one copy of the base model and load small adapters on demand. Requests for different adapters can share a batch using specialized kernels: Punica introduced batched multi-adapter kernels (Chen et al., 2023), and S-LoRA showed thousands of adapters served from one GPU with unified paging of adapter weights and KV cache (Sheng et al., 2023). vLLM and SGLang support multi-LoRA with a configurable number of resident adapters and LRU eviction.

  • This makes per-tenant fine-tunes economically realistic: a ~100 MB adapter per customer instead of a GPU per customer.
  • Route with adapter affinity so hot adapters stay resident, and set a cold-load latency budget (loading a ~100 MB adapter from host memory takes milliseconds; from object storage longer).
  • Higher ranks and many distinct adapters per batch add some overhead; measure.

Evaluation, forgetting and safety

  • Task evals: the metric you fine-tuned for, on the frozen eval set, compared with the prompted baseline and the teacher.
  • Regression evals: general capability, instruction following, and other tasks the model must still do. Narrow fine-tunes cause catastrophic forgetting; mitigate with LoRA, lower learning rates, fewer epochs, and mixing some general data into training.
  • Safety evals: fine-tuning can erode a model's safety behavior, even with benign data (Qi et al., 2023). Re-run refusal and policy tests on every fine-tuned model.
  • Calibration and abstention: check that the model still says "I don't know" or escalates where it should.

Versioning and rollout

  • Registry entry per model: base model and version, adapter, dataset hashes, hyperparameters, training code commit, eval report. Treat it like a build artifact.
  • Rollout: shadow traffic (score without serving), then a small canary, then A/B against the incumbent on online metrics, with instant rollback by routing.
  • Base model churn: hosted base models get deprecated and open models get better every few months. Keep the data pipeline and eval suite reproducible so re-tuning on a new base is a routine job, not a project.
  • Continuous improvement: production failures flow back into the dataset (the eval flywheel); retrain on a schedule or when the failure backlog justifies it.

Fine-tuning in System Design Interviews

When to bring it up

  • When cost or latency of a frontier model is the problem at high volume: "Once we have a few months of labeled traffic, I'd distill this classifier into a small model."
  • When behavior is inconsistent despite prompt work: "If the format failure rate stays above our threshold, a LoRA fine-tune on a few thousand corrected examples is the next step."
  • When a multi-tenant product needs per-customer behavior: "Per-tenant LoRA adapters on a shared base, served with multi-LoRA batching."
  • When retrieval quality is the bottleneck: "Fine-tune the reranker on click and feedback data before touching the generator."

When not to

  • The problem is missing or changing knowledge (use RAG).
  • There's no eval set to prove improvement.
  • You can't get a few hundred high-quality examples.
  • Requirements change weekly (prompts iterate in minutes; fine-tunes in days).

How to introduce it

  1. State the measured gap: which metric, current value, target.
  2. Show that cheaper rungs were tried or why they can't work.
  3. Describe the data: source, volume, labeling, cleaning, frozen eval split.
  4. Pick the method (SFT with LoRA by default; DPO for preferences; RL with verifiable rewards when outputs can be checked automatically) and the base model size.
  5. Explain serving (merged vs multi-LoRA) and the cost and latency gain.
  6. Close with evals, regression and safety checks, rollout and the retraining loop.

Common deep-dive questions

"Our support bot gives outdated policy answers. Should we fine-tune on the policy docs?"

Bad Solution
Fine-tune the model on the policy documents

Challenges: facts are memorized unreliably, can't be cited, and are stale again the next time the policy changes; every update means retraining and re-evaluating.

Good Solution
RAG over versioned policy documents

Approach: index the policies with version and effective-date metadata, retrieve the current version, require citations.

Challenges: answers can still drift in tone or format, and retrieval may miss the right section.

Great Solution
RAG for knowledge, optional fine-tunes for behavior and retrieval

Approach: RAG with freshness via change events and effective-date filters; fine-tune the reranker on feedback to fix retrieval misses; only if tone or format stays inconsistent, LoRA-tune the generator on approved answers; gate everything on a golden set of policy questions.

Challenges: more moving parts; needs ownership of the eval set as policies change.

How would you serve custom models for 2,000 enterprise customers?

Per-customer LoRA adapters on a shared base, multi-LoRA serving with an adapter cache, adapter-affinity routing, per-tenant eval gates before activation, and a fallback to the base model if an adapter fails to load or regresses.

How much data do you need?

It depends on the task: hundreds to low thousands of curated examples for format and style; thousands to tens of thousands for narrow classification and extraction; far more for new capabilities. Then say how you'd find out: train on increasing subsets and plot the eval metric; stop when it plateaus.

How do you know the fine-tune didn't break something else?

Regression suite on general capability and other product tasks, safety and refusal tests, shadow traffic comparison, canary with online metrics, and rollback by routing.

DPO or RL?

DPO when you have preference pairs and subjective goals; RL with verifiable rewards when a program can grade outputs (tests, exact answers, schema checks). Both need SFT first in most pipelines and a strong eval suite to catch reward hacking.

Summary

  • Climb the ladder: prompting, examples and RAG first; fine-tune when evals show a behavior, cost or latency gap they can't close.
  • LoRA is the default: ~0.5% of parameters at r = 16, cheap to train, hot-swappable at serving time.
  • Distillation from a big model into a small one is the most common business case.
  • Data quality, frozen eval sets and lineage matter more than training tricks.
  • Multi-LoRA serving makes per-tenant models practical; registries, regression and safety evals, and canaries make them safe.

Related: Evaluation for building the eval sets, Inference & Serving for serving engines, and RAG in Depth for when retrieval is the better answer.

LLM System Design · Core Concepts

Numbers to Know

The reference figures and formulas behind capacity, latency and cost estimates for LLM systems, followed by five fully worked estimates you can adapt in an interview.

Classic system design has its "latency numbers every programmer should know." LLM systems add a new set: tokens per word, KV bytes per token, GPU bandwidth, dollars per million tokens. Interviewers rarely care whether you remember an exact figure; they care whether you can turn a product requirement into tokens per second, then into GPUs or dollars, and spot which number drives the design.

Prices and hardware specs move fast. Figures here are rounded and were checked in November 2026. Hardware specs come from vendor datasheets; API prices are given as bands. Quote orders of magnitude in interviews, and check the official pricing pages before using a number for a real budget.

Tokens and text

QuantityRule of thumb
English text1 token ≈ 4 characters ≈ 0.75 words; 1,000 words ≈ 1,300 tokens. Varies by tokenizer: Claude 4.7 and later produce ~30% more tokens for the same text
A page of prose~500 words ≈ 650–700 tokens
A 300-page book~100K words ≈ 130K tokens
Source codeMore tokens per character than prose (whitespace, symbols); budget ~8–12 tokens per line
Non-English textOften 1.5–3× the tokens of the English equivalent, depending on language and tokenizer
Speech~150 spoken words/min ≈ 200 tokens/min ≈ 12K tokens per hour of audio transcript
Images (Claude)≈ (width ÷ 28) × (height ÷ 28) tokens, one per 28×28-pixel patch; a 1000×1000 image ≈ 1,296 tokens, and large images are downscaled to a per-model cap (vision docs). Other providers use tile-based formulas of a similar magnitude.
Chat turn in a productInput 2K–10K tokens (system prompt, history, retrieved context, tools); output 100–800
Agent stepInput grows each step (10K → 100K+), output 100–1,000 per step

Time

Converting rates

1 day   = 86,400 s ≈ 10^5 s           1 month ≈ 2.6M s ≈ 30 days
1M requests/day  ≈ 12 req/s average   100M requests/day ≈ 1,160 req/s
peak ≈ 2–3 × average for consumer traffic (higher for spiky B2B or launch days)

Latency of each pipeline stage

OperationRough latency
Network round trip, same region / cross-continent~1 ms / 70–150 ms
Redis GET; indexed Postgres query< 1 ms; 1–10 ms
Embedding a query (self-hosted small model / hosted API)~5–20 ms / ~50–200 ms

Cross-encoder reranking of 50–100 candidates~50–200 ms
Small-model classification call (router, guard)~50–300 ms
Time to first token, hosted API~0.2–2 s (longer for long prompts and under load)
Decode speed per stream~30–150 tok/s typical; small or speculative setups faster
Reasoning ("thinking") phaseSeconds to minutes, depending on effort budget
Web search API call~0.3–2 s
Streaming speech-to-text final transcript after end of speech~100–300 ms
Text-to-speech time to first audio~100–300 ms
MicroVM / sandbox start from snapshot~100 ms to a few seconds
Human reading speed~4–5 words/s (≈ 5–7 tok/s), so 20+ tok/s streaming feels instant
Natural gap between speakers in conversation~200 ms (Stivers et al., PNAS 2009)

Two derived numbers matter most: bandwidth sets decode speed and HBM sets how many tokens of KV cache you can hold. See Inference & Serving for why.

weight bytes = parameters × bytes per parameter
  FP32 = 4    BF16/FP16 = 2    FP8/INT8 = 1    INT4/FP4 ≈ 0.5 (+ small scale overhead)
Model sizeBF16FP8INT4Minimum practical GPUs (BF16 / FP8)
8B16 GB8 GB4 GB1 / 1 (runs on a laptop at INT4)

KV cache per token (FP16)

ModelShapeKV / token128K-token context
Llama 3 8B32 layers, 8 KV heads, dim 128128 KB16 GB
Llama 3 70B / Qwen-2.5 72B80 layers, 8 KV heads, dim 128320 KB40 GB
Llama 3.1 405B126 layers, 8 KV heads, dim 128516 KB66 GB

Sizes use binary units (320 KB = 327,680 bytes, which papers often round to 327 KB). Halve these with an FP8 KV cache. Reserve another ~10–20% of HBM for activations, CUDA graphs, framework overhead and fragmentation.

KV capacity (tokens) ≈ (total HBM × 0.9 − weight bytes) ÷ KV bytes per token
8 × H100, Llama 3 70B FP16:  (640 × 0.9 − 140) GB ÷ 320 KB ≈ 1.3M tokens
concurrent sequences ≈ KV capacity ÷ average live context length

Training memory (for fine-tuning questions)

full fine-tune with Adam, mixed precision ≈ 16 bytes/param + activations
  (2 weights + 2 grads + 4 FP32 master + 8 Adam moments)
  7B → ~112 GB   70B → ~1.1 TB  (shard with FSDP/ZeRO)
LoRA: frozen base (2 bytes/param, or ~0.5 with QLoRA) + tiny adapter states

Details in Fine-tuning & Adaptation.

Vector storage

raw vector bytes = count × dimensions × bytes per dimension
Vectors (1,024 dims)float32int8 / scalar quantizedbinary
1M4.1 GB1 GB128 MB
100M410 GB102 GB13 GB
1B4.1 TB1 TB128 GB

Add index overhead (an HNSW graph with M=16 stores roughly 32 neighbor IDs per vector on the base layer, ~130 bytes or more), metadata, and the chunk text itself. More in Embeddings & Vector Search.

Throughput and cost

Formulas

API cost per request = in_tokens × in_price + out_tokens × out_price
                     − cached_in_tokens × in_price × (1 − cache_read_multiplier)

decode throughput (per replica) ≈ batch × 1 ÷ step_time
step_time ≈ (weight bytes + KV bytes read) ÷ HBM bandwidth     // lower bound
prefill time ≈ 2 × params × prompt_tokens ÷ (FLOP/s × MFU)      // MFU ~40–60%

self-hosted $ per 1M output tokens = (GPUs × $/GPU-hour) ÷ (tokens/s × 3,600) × 10^6 ÷ utilization

Example: one 8×H100 node at $3 per GPU-hour costs $24/hour. If it sustains 5,000 output tok/s at your latency SLO, that's 18M tokens/hour, or $1.33 per 1M output tokens at 100% utilization, and $3.33 at a more realistic 40% average utilization. GPU rental prices vary widely by provider, commitment and generation, so treat $/GPU-hour as an input to state, not a constant.

API price bands (November 2026)

TierInput $/1M tokensOutput $/1M tokensUse for
Small / fast~0.05–1~0.40–5Routing, classification, extraction, summaries, guards
Mid-tier~0.25–3~2–15Most product features, RAG answers, agents
Frontier~2–15~10–75Hardest reasoning, coding, high-stakes answers
Embeddings~0.02–0.20n/aIndexing and query embedding
  • Output costs ~4–8× input per token on most models.
  • Prompt cache reads cost ~0.1× base input on most Anthropic models (0.05× or less on the newest; writes 1.25× for the 5-minute cache), with similar large discounts elsewhere.
  • Batch APIs are typically 50% off for work that can wait up to 24 hours.
  • Very long prompts may be billed at a higher rate past a context threshold on some models.
  • Premium "pro" tiers and fast modes are priced well above these bands.

Check current figures: Claude pricing, OpenAI pricing, Gemini pricing. Bands are rounded from these pages and third-party trackers in November 2026.

The estimation method

  1. Start from users and actions, not requests: DAU × actions per user per day.
  2. Convert to requests/s (÷ 86,400) and apply a peak factor.
  3. Convert to tokens/s, separately for input and output, and note how much input is cacheable.
  4. Split by phase: input tokens drive prefill compute (or API input cost); output tokens drive decode time, KV residency and output cost.
  5. Turn into GPUs or dollars, add headroom (N+1 replicas, 30–50% for spikes), then sanity-check against something you know.

Say your assumptions out loud and round aggressively (2,000 not 1,873). The interviewer is grading whether the number changes a decision: "that's $3M a month on the frontier API, so routing 70% of turns to a small model is worth the complexity."

Worked estimates

1) GPUs for a 1M-DAU chat product on a self-hosted 70B model

Traffic:   1M DAU × 10 messages/day = 10M requests/day ≈ 116 req/s, peak ×3 ≈ 350 req/s
Tokens:    input 2,000 (history; ~50% prefix-cached), output 400
Decode:    350 × 400 = 140K output tok/s at peak
           realistic node (8×H100, FP16, TPOT ≤ 30 ms) ≈ 5,000 output tok/s
           → 140K ÷ 5K ≈ 28 nodes
Prefill:   350 × 2,000 × 50% uncached = 350K tok/s
           2 × 70e9 × 350e3 ≈ 4.9e16 FLOP/s ÷ (8 × 989e12 × 0.5 ≈ 4e15 per node) ≈ 12 nodes of compute
           decode leaves most compute idle, so chunked prefill absorbs much of this on the same nodes
KV check:  concurrent streams ≈ 350 req/s × (400 ÷ 30 tok/s ≈ 13 s) ≈ 4,700
           per node ≈ 4,700 ÷ 30 ≈ 160 streams × ~2.4K tokens ≈ 380K tokens ≪ 1.3M capacity ✓
Answer:    ~30–40 nodes at peak + headroom ≈ 40–45 nodes (320–360 H100s)
Cost:      40 × 8 × $3 ≈ $960/hour at peak; autoscaled average ~half ≈ $350K/month

Sanity check against an API: 10M requests/day at a mid-tier price ($2 in, $10 out per million) is roughly $40K/day of uncached input (less with caching) plus $40K/day of output, around $2.4M/month. That gap is why high-volume products move some traffic to self-hosted or smaller models, though the comparison only holds if the open model meets the quality bar.

2) Monthly cost of a RAG support assistant on an API

Traffic:   50K conversations/day × 4 turns = 200K turns/day ≈ 6M turns/month
Per turn:  system prompt + tool definitions 3K (cached) + retrieved chunks 3K
           + history 1K + question 100 ≈ 7.1K input; 300 output
Price:     mid-tier $2/M in, $10/M out (Sonnet 5.5), cache reads 0.05×
Input:     3K × 0.05 + 4.1K = 4.25K effective × $2/M ≈ $0.0085
Output:    300 × $10/M ≈ $0.003
Extras:    query rewrite on a small model, embeddings, rerank ≈ $0.001
Per turn ≈ $0.0125 → per conversation ≈ $0.05 → ≈ $75K/month

Levers, in order of impact: cut retrieved context (better reranking, fewer chunks), route simple FAQ turns to a small model, shorten answers, raise the cached share of the prompt. See the support assistant breakdown.

3) Embedding and storing a 50M-document corpus

Corpus:    50M docs × 2,000 tokens = 100B tokens
Chunks:    500-token chunks, 10% overlap → ≈ 220M chunks
API cost:  100B × $0.02/M ≈ $2,000 (≈ $1,000 via batch)
Rate:      at 10M tokens/min of quota → 10,000 min ≈ 7 days   // quota, not dollars, is the constraint
Self-host: 2 × 335M params × 100e9 tokens ≈ 6.7e19 FLOPs
           ÷ (989e12 × 30% MFU ≈ 3e14) ≈ 2.2e5 s ≈ 62 H100-hours → a few hours on 16 GPUs
Storage:   220M × 1,024 × 4 B ≈ 900 GB float32; ≈ 225 GB int8; ≈ 28 GB binary
           + HNSW graph (~30–60 GB) + chunk text (~400 GB) + metadata

Decisions this drives: shard the index (or use a disk-based index with quantized vectors in RAM), keep full-precision vectors on disk for rescoring, and plan re-embedding (a model upgrade means paying all of this again). See Embeddings & Vector Search.

4) Cost of one coding-agent run

Run:       40 steps; context grows 10K → 80K (average 45K input per step); 500 output per step
Input:     40 × 45K = 1.8M tokens
  no caching:     1.8M × $2/M ≈ $3.60
  with caching:   ~90% of each step's input is a cache hit
                  1.8M × (0.9 × 0.05 + 0.1 × 1.25) ≈ 0.31M effective ≈ $0.61
Output:    40 × 500 = 20K × $10/M ≈ $0.20
Total ≈ $0.81 per run with caching vs ≈ $3.80 without; sandbox minutes are cents

Input dominates and grows roughly quadratically with step count because every step resends the history. That is why agents rely on prompt caching, tool-output truncation, compaction and sub-agents (Context Engineering, Design Claude Code).

5) Voice agent latency budget

Target: reply audio starts < ~1 s after the user stops talking (humans: ~200 ms gaps)

End-of-turn detection (VAD + endpointing)   200–500 ms   // the biggest, most tunable chunk
Final STT transcript                        100–300 ms   (overlaps with endpointing when streaming)
LLM time to first token                     300–700 ms   (small/fast model, short prompt, cached prefix)
First sentence of text (~15 tokens)          ~100–300 ms
TTS time to first audio                     100–250 ms
Network (client ↔ server, both ways)         50–150 ms
Total ≈ 0.9–2.2 s naive; ≈ 0.7–1.0 s with streaming at every stage and tight endpointing

Every stage must stream into the next. Speech-to-speech models collapse STT, LLM and TTS into one model and remove some of these hops. See Real-time Voice Agent.

Numbers in System Design Interviews

When to estimate

  • Right after non-functional requirements, when scale shapes the architecture: "Let me size this quickly, because whether we need a GPU fleet or an API budget changes the design."
  • When choosing between options: model tiers, self-host vs API, RAG vs long context.
  • When the interviewer pushes on cost or latency in a deep dive.

How to keep it fast

  1. Memorize a few anchors: 4 chars/token, 10^5 s/day, H100 = 80 GB and 3.35 TB/s, 70B FP16 = 140 GB, 320 KB KV/token for 70B, output ≈ 5× input price, cache reads ≈ 0.05–0.1×.
  2. Write the chain on the board (users → req/s → tokens/s → GPUs or $) so the interviewer can follow and correct assumptions.
  3. Compute only what decides something. If the answer is "fits on one node" or "costs $500/month," move on.
  4. Finish with the implication: "so prompt caching is mandatory," "so we need to shard the index," "so the small model handles the first pass."

Common mistakes

  • Counting requests instead of tokens (one agent request can be 100× a chat turn).
  • Forgetting that conversation history makes input grow every turn.
  • Sizing GPUs by compute when KV memory or bandwidth is the binding constraint.
  • Using sparse TFLOP/s figures from marketing material.
  • Ignoring rate limits and quotas, which often bind before budget does.

Summary

Convert everything to tokens, split input from output, and know the handful of hardware anchors that turn tokens into seconds and dollars. Then let the numbers drive decisions: caching, routing, sharding, self-hosting. For the mechanisms behind these figures read Inference & Serving; for where they show up in practice, see the worked examples.

Question Breakdown · Hard

Design Claude Code (an AI Coding Harness)

An agentic coding tool that runs in the developer's terminal or IDE, reads and edits the local repository, runs commands, and asks before doing anything risky. Representative of "design Claude Code / Codex CLI / Gemini CLI" and the broader "design an agent harness" prompt.

Understanding the Problem

A developer opens a terminal in their repository and types "the date parser test is flaky, find out why and fix it." The tool explores the code, reads the test, runs it a few times, edits two files, re-runs the tests, and reports back, streaming every step so the developer can interrupt or redirect it. The model does the thinking; everything around the model is the harness: the loop that calls the model, the tools it can use, the context it sees, the rules about what it may do, and the extension points teams use to customize it.

The interesting part of this problem is that the hard engineering is not scale in the usual sense. The harness runs on one laptop for one user. The hard parts are: giving a model good-enough context about a huge codebase through a finite window, letting it run real shell commands on a machine that holds the user's SSH keys and cloud credentials, keeping long sessions affordable, and making edits that never silently corrupt code.

How this differs from the cloud coding agent

The AI Coding Agent breakdown is "issue in, pull request out" in a cloud sandbox. Clarify early which one the interviewer wants. The differences drive the whole design:

Local harness (this page)Cloud coding agent
Where code runsThe developer's own machine, with their files, credentials and networkA disposable microVM per run
InteractionSynchronous, human watching and steering turn by turnAsynchronous, human reviews a PR at the end
Main riskDamaging or leaking the user's machine and secretsTenant isolation, runaway cost across thousands of runs
Safety modelPermission prompts, rules, modes, OS-level sandboxVM isolation, egress proxy, credentials outside the sandbox
StateLocal transcript and file checkpointsDurable workflow history in a server
Scale problemContext and cost per session; the backend is the model APIScheduling sandboxes and warm pools for 10K concurrent runs

Functional Requirements

  1. Developers should be able to give a natural-language task in an interactive terminal session, watch the agent's text, tool calls and diffs stream live, and interrupt or steer at any time.
  2. The agent should be able to explore the codebase, edit files, and run commands (build, tests, git, package managers) on the developer's machine.
  3. Developers and organizations should control what the agent may do without asking: per-tool rules, permission modes, and managed policy.
  4. Sessions should persist: resume a past conversation, and rewind file changes the agent made.
  5. Teams should be able to extend it: project instructions, custom commands, deterministic hooks, external tools over MCP, skills and specialized subagents.
  6. The same engine should run headless (a CLI flag or an SDK) for CI and scripted automation.

Below the line: training the model, running the inference fleet (see Inference Batching), cloud sandboxes (see AI Coding Agent), keystroke-level autocomplete (see Copilot-style Autocomplete), billing.

Non-Functional Requirements

  1. Responsiveness: the UI reacts to keystrokes and Esc within ~100 ms; the first streamed token of a turn arrives in ~1–2 s; local tools such as search and read return in tens of milliseconds.
  2. Safety: nothing destructive or outward-facing happens without consent or an explicit rule; a hijacked agent's blast radius is bounded by OS enforcement, not by the model behaving well.
  3. Local-first privacy: code leaves the machine only as context sent to the model API (optionally through the customer's own cloud provider); no repository index is uploaded.
  4. Works on huge repos: millions of lines, no pre-built index required, startup in about a second.
  5. Affordable long sessions: 50–200 model calls per session must not cost dollars per step; target a prompt-cache hit rate above 90% of input tokens.
  6. Reliability: a crash, network drop or Ctrl-C never leaves a half-written file; sessions are resumable; transient API errors are retried with backoff.
  7. Cross-platform: macOS, Linux and Windows, many shells and terminals.

The Set Up

Core Entities

  • Session: id, working directory, model, permission mode, token and cost counters.
  • Message: user text, assistant text, tool_use and tool_result blocks; the ordered list of messages is the agent's state.
  • Tool: name, description, JSON schema, read-only or mutating, concurrency-safe or not.
  • ToolCall: tool, arguments, permission decision, result (possibly truncated), duration.
  • PermissionRule: allow, ask or deny, a tool pattern such as Bash(npm run test:*) or Read(./.env), and the scope it came from (managed, command line, local, project, user).
  • Hook: lifecycle event, matcher, command to run, timeout.
  • Subagent: name, description, system prompt, allowed tools, model.
  • Skill: folder with a SKILL.md (name, description, instructions) plus optional scripts and reference files.
  • MCP server: transport (stdio or HTTP), command or URL, credentials, the tools and resources it exposes.
  • Checkpoint: snapshot of files before an edit, tied to a message, so code and conversation can be rewound together.

Interface

The "API" here is two surfaces: the CLI the developer uses, and the model API the harness calls. Claude Code's public CLI looks like this:

claude                                   # interactive session in the current repo
claude "fix the flaky date parser test"  # start with a first prompt
claude --continue | --resume <session>   # reload a past transcript
claude -p "summarize this diff" --output-format stream-json --verbose  # headless, scriptable
/compact  /rewind  /permissions  /agents  /mcp                         # in-session slash commands

Underneath, every step of the agent is one streaming call to a tool-use API:

POST /v1/messages   stream: true
{ system:   [ ...harness prompt..., cache_control ],      // stable, cached
  tools:    [ Read, Edit, Write, Glob, Grep, Bash, ... ],  // stable, cached
  messages: [ user, assistant(tool_use), user(tool_result), ... ] }
→ SSE: text deltas, tool_use input deltas,
       stop_reason: "tool_use" | "end_turn",
       usage: { input_tokens, cache_read_input_tokens, cache_creation_input_tokens, output_tokens }

Edit { file_path, old_string, new_string, replace_all? }
  // in this design: fails if the file wasn't read this session, changed since it was read,
  // or old_string is not unique

Back-of-envelope: tokens and cost per session

Assume one session of 40 model calls. The stable prefix (system prompt, tool definitions, memory) is ~20K tokens; the conversation grows to ~100K, so the average call carries ~60K input tokens and writes ~300 output tokens. Prices are Sonnet 5.5 list prices: $2 per million input and $10 per million output tokens, with cache writes at 1.25× and cache reads at 0.05× of input (Claude pricing; check current numbers before quoting).

input processed  = 40 calls × 60K           = 2.4M tokens
output           = 40 × 300                 = 12K tokens  → $0.12

no caching:      2.4M × $2/M                = $4.80  (+ $0.12) ≈ $4.90 / session
with caching:    new tokens written ≈ 100K × $2.50/M  = $0.25
                 reads ≈ 2.3M × $0.10/M               = $0.23
                 total (+ output)                     ≈ $0.60 / session
cache hit rate   ≈ 2.3M / 2.4M                         ≈ 96%

fleet: 1M developers × 3 sessions/day × 2.4M = 7.2T input tokens/day
       uncached share ~4% → ~0.3T tokens/day of real prefill (~3.5M tokens/s)
       output: 1M × 3 × 12K = 36B tokens/day (~420K tokens/s)

Two conclusions shape the design. First, agent loops are input-heavy: each step re-sends the whole conversation, so prompt caching cuts session cost roughly 8× and the harness must be built to keep the cache warm. Second, anything that rewrites early context (editing old messages, reordering tools, a timestamp in the system prompt) silently multiplies cost. See Caching for LLMs and Inference & Serving for the provider-side mechanics.

High-Level Design

1) Interactive tasks: the agent loop

The core is deliberately simple: one loop, one message list. Anthropic describes the loop behind Claude Code and its Agent SDK as gather context → take action → verify work → repeat (Building agents with the Claude Agent SDK). One reasonable implementation:

  1. The user submits a prompt; it is appended to the message list.
  2. The context manager builds the request (system prompt, tools, memory, messages) and checks the token count; if it is near the limit, it compacts first.
  3. The loop streams the model response, rendering text deltas immediately and buffering tool_use blocks.
  4. If the response ends with end_turn, the turn is over and control returns to the user.
  5. Otherwise, each tool call goes through the permission pipeline and runs. Read-only, concurrency-safe calls (several greps or reads) can run in parallel; mutating calls run one at a time in order.
  6. Results, truncated to a budget, are appended as tool_result blocks, and the loop goes back to step 2.

Why a single-threaded master loop rather than a graph of agents? Debuggability and predictability: the transcript is a complete, linear record of what happened, every decision is visible to the user, and there is exactly one place where budgets, interrupts and permissions are enforced. Parallelism is added in controlled places (parallel read-only tools, subagents) instead of everywhere.

Interrupts and steering. Esc aborts the HTTP stream and sends SIGINT/SIGTERM to any running child process, then appends a marker ("the user interrupted") so the model knows its last action may be incomplete. A message typed while the agent is working is queued and injected at the next step boundary, never mid-tool, so tool_use/tool_result pairs stay well-formed.

2) Exploring, editing and running

The model can only act through tools, so tool design is product design. Anthropic's guidance: a small set of clearly distinct tools, outputs that are token-efficient (truncation, pagination, sensible defaults), and error messages that tell the model how to recover (Writing effective tools for agents). A typical set:

ToolPurposeDesign notes
Glob, GrepFind files and textGrep is ripgrep and skips gitignored files; return paths first, matches with context only on request, capped. Claude Code now includes both by default only on Windows; on macOS, Linux and WSL it searches with embedded find and grep through Bash
ReadRead a file or a line rangeLine numbers in output so edits can be precise; large files paginated; images and PDFs supported
Edit, WriteChange filesExact-string replacement; read-before-edit and staleness checks (deep dive 4)
BashBuild, test, git, anythingTimeout, output truncated head and tail, long-running processes as background tasks; sandboxed (deep dive 2)
WebFetch, WebSearchDocs and error lookupsContent is untrusted; summarized before entering context
Agent (subagent)Delegate exploration or a side jobRuns a fresh loop with its own context; returns a short report
TaskCreate, TaskUpdate (replaced TodoWrite)Plan and track stepsKeeps multi-step work on track and visible to the user; Claude Code enables them by default only on older models, since newer ones track multi-step work without a written checklist

What the model sees on every call is assembled by the context manager. The order matters as much as the content, because the provider caches by exact prefix:

Memory files. Claude Code loads CLAUDE.md files at launch from the directory hierarchy above the working directory (plus a user-level file and organization-managed policy), and loads CLAUDE.md files in subdirectories on demand when the agent reads files there (Claude Code memory docs). Codex CLI does the same with AGENTS.md. These files are the team's curated map: build and test commands, conventions, "never touch the generated folder." They are paid for on every call, so they should be short.

3) Controlling what the agent may do

Every tool call passes through a permission engine before it runs. Claude Code checks each call in a fixed order: PreToolUse hooks, deny rules, ask rules, the permission mode, allow rules, and finally a prompt (the canUseTool callback in the Agent SDK) for anything still undecided (Agent SDK permissions):

  • Rules are patterns per tool: allow Bash(npm run test:*), ask for Bash(git push:*), deny Read(./.env). Deny always wins.
  • Scopes layer, highest precedence first: organization-managed settings (which nothing can override), command-line arguments, personal local project overrides, shared project settings checked into the repo, then user settings. Rule lists merge across scopes, so a deny from any scope still wins.
  • Modes set the default for everything the rules don't cover: ask for anything that changes state; auto-accept file edits; plan mode (read-only research and a proposed plan, no edits); a classifier-reviewed auto mode; and a bypass mode meant only for throwaway containers.
  • Hooks are the deterministic escape hatch: a PreToolUse hook can block a call (exit code 2, with stderr fed back to the model) regardless of mode (hooks reference).

Rules alone are not a security boundary, which is the subject of deep dive 2.

4) Sessions, resume and rewind

Each session is an append-only transcript on local disk (Claude Code keeps them per project under ~/.claude/projects). Append-only matters twice: a crash loses at most the in-flight step, and resume is just "reload the messages and continue," which also keeps the prompt-cache prefix identical. Before an edit the harness snapshots the affected file into a checkpoint tied to the user prompt that started the turn; /rewind restores code, conversation, or both to that point.

Checkpoints only track files the agent edited through its file tools. A Bash command that deletes other files, runs a migration or pushes to a remote is outside them. Say this in the interview: git (and the permission system) is the real safety net for shell side effects, and the harness should encourage committing before risky steps.

5) Extensibility and 6) headless mode

Extension points (hooks, MCP, skills, subagents, slash commands, plugins) plug into the same loop and are covered in deep dive 5. Headless mode is the same engine without the TUI: claude -p reads a prompt, runs the loop, and emits text or a JSON event stream; the Agent SDK exposes the loop as a library. Because nobody is there to answer a permission prompt, everything the run may do must be declared up front (deep dive 6). Putting it together:

Everything except the model API runs on the developer's machine. That is the defining property: the harness has the user's full local power, and the design's job is to channel that power safely.

Potential Deep Dives

1) How does the agent find the right code in a huge repo?

Bad Solution
Put the repository (or as much as fits) in the prompt

Challenges: real repos are millions of tokens; even a 1M-token window would cost dollars per step and bury the relevant lines. Model accuracy degrades as context fills with irrelevant text ("context rot," Anthropic).

Good Solution
Embedding index of code chunks, retrieved per task

Approach: chunk by function or class, embed, store in a local or hosted vector index, retrieve the top-k chunks for each query.

Challenges: indexing a monorepo takes minutes and must be kept fresh as the agent itself edits files; uploading embeddings or code to a service conflicts with local-first privacy; semantic similarity misses exact identifiers, call sites and config keys; retrieved chunks lack the surrounding context an engineer would read.

Great Solution
Agentic search: fast tools, a curated map, and subagents

Approach: give the model the same tools an engineer uses (glob, ripgrep, read with line ranges, git log/blame through Bash) and let it search iteratively: grep for the error string, read the test, follow the import. The CLAUDE.md file acts as a hand-written map of the repo. For broad questions ("how does auth work across these services?") the agent spawns a subagent that explores in its own context and returns a 1–2K-token summary, so the main context stays clean. Anthropic recommends starting with agentic search and adding semantic search only if you need faster results, because it is more accurate, easier to maintain and more transparent (Agent SDK post). A semantic or LSP-backed tool can still be added over MCP.

Challenges: more model calls per task (mitigated by prompt caching and cheap, fast tools), and quality depends heavily on tool output design: a grep that returns 5,000 lines is worse than none.

2) How do we let it run shell commands safely on a developer's laptop?

The threat model has two parts: the model making a mistake (rm -rf in the wrong directory, force-pushing), and prompt injection, where text in a README, issue, dependency or web page instructs the agent to exfiltrate ~/.ssh or .env. Simon Willison's "lethal trifecta" frames it: private data + untrusted content + a way to communicate externally. A coding agent has all three by default, so the design must cut at least one leg.

Bad Solution
Ask for approval on every command, or approve everything

Challenges: constant prompts train users to click yes; Anthropic's telemetry showed users approved roughly 93% of permission prompts, and attention drops as approvals pile up (Anthropic, How we contain Claude). Approving everything removes the only check.

Good Solution
Allow/deny rules, permission modes and plan mode

Approach: safe, frequent commands (tests, linters, read-only git) are allow-listed; pushes and deploys always ask; secrets files are denied; plan mode lets the agent research without changing anything.

Challenges: rules match strings, but shells are programmable. npm test runs whatever package.json says, a build script can curl anywhere, and a prefix rule like git:* also allows options that execute commands. Rules reduce mistakes; they don't contain an adversary.

Great Solution
OS-level sandbox for filesystem and network, with prompts only at the boundary

Approach: run Bash and every child process inside an OS sandbox: Seatbelt on macOS, bubblewrap on Linux and WSL2 (Claude Code sandboxing docs). Writes are allowed only inside the project directory and a temp directory; sensitive paths can be blocked for reads; network traffic goes through a proxy outside the sandbox that only allows approved domains (package registries, the git host). Inside the boundary, commands run without prompts; anything that needs to cross it asks. Anthropic reports that sandboxing cut permission prompts by 84% in internal use (Anthropic, sandboxing post) and open-sourced the runtime. OpenAI's Codex CLI takes the same approach with Seatbelt on macOS and bubblewrap on Linux and WSL2 (Codex docs). Both legs matter: without network isolation a compromised agent can exfiltrate keys; without filesystem isolation it can modify shell config or other system files to get network access later.

Layer the rest on top: enterprise-managed deny rules users can't override; hooks for org policy (block edits to .github/workflows, scan commands for secrets); the model API key and other credentials never placed in context; and, for fewer interruptions outside the sandbox, a separate classifier model that reviews each proposed action before it runs, as Claude Code's auto mode does (Simon Willison's write-up).

Challenges: platform gaps (WSL1 and some container setups lack the needed kernel features, so the harness must detect that and fall back to stricter prompting); allowlisted domains can still be abused (a package registry is a place to upload data), so keep the list tight; tools that legitimately need broad access (Docker, cloud CLIs) need explicit, visible exceptions.

3) How do we manage the context window over a two-hour session?

Bad Solution
Drop the oldest messages when the window fills

Challenges: the oldest messages contain the task itself and the key decisions; dropping them can orphan tool_use/tool_result pairs (an API error), and every drop changes the prefix, so the cache misses on every subsequent call.

Good Solution
Summarize the history near the limit and cap tool outputs

Approach: when usage crosses a threshold, ask the model to summarize the conversation, replace the history with the summary, and continue. Truncate long tool outputs to a fixed budget.

Challenges: naive summaries lose file paths, exact error messages and the user's constraints; the agent then repeats work or violates an instruction it no longer sees.

Great Solution
Prevent, offload, externalize, then compact with structure, all cache-aware

Approach:

  • Prevent bloat: tools return compact output by default (paths before contents, head and tail of logs, pagination), so a test run costs 2K tokens, not 40K.
  • Offload: subagents explore in their own context window and return short findings; the parent never sees the 30 files they read.
  • Externalize state: a todo list, notes files and CLAUDE.md hold plans and decisions outside the window, and are re-read after compaction.
  • Compact with a schema: the summary keeps the user's goal and constraints, decisions made, files modified, open tasks and the last errors verbatim; recently read files are re-attached. Users can trigger it manually (/compact with instructions) at a natural breakpoint.
  • Stay cache-friendly: the history is append-only; the system prompt and tool list are byte-stable (no timestamps or random ordering at the top); cache breakpoints sit at the end of the stable prefix and at the latest turn. Compaction is one deliberate cache break, not a stream of small ones.

Challenges: the default 5-minute cache lifetime means a developer who reads a diff for ten minutes pays a cache write on the next step (a 1-hour cache tier exists at a higher write price); compaction quality needs its own evals.

Session (40 calls, avg 60K context)Input costRelative
No caching$7.201×
Caching, append-only history≈ $1.07≈ 0.15×
Caching, but a timestamp at the top of the system prompt≈ $9.001.25× (every call is a cache write)

Derived from the session estimate above. The last row is the trap: a cache that never hits is more expensive than no cache.

4) How do we make edits reliable?

Bad Solution
The model rewrites the whole file

Challenges: an 800-line file is ~10K output tokens: at ~60 tokens/s that is close to three minutes and ~$0.15 per edit, versus a few seconds for a 20-line change. Models also "helpfully" elide unchanged code (// ... rest unchanged) and silently drop functions.

Good Solution
Diffs or patches

Approach: the model emits a unified diff or a patch format with context anchors (Codex CLI uses an apply_patch tool with its own format). Output is small and multi-hunk changes are one call.

Challenges: models miscount line numbers and context lines; patches fail to apply after the file drifts, and fuzzy application can apply a hunk in the wrong place.

Great Solution
Exact-string replace with guardrails, feedback and checkpoints

Approach: Edit(old_string, new_string) must match exactly once, so ambiguity becomes an error the model can fix by including more surrounding lines. The harness enforces read-before-edit (the model must have seen the current content) and staleness detection (if the file's hash or mtime changed since the last read, because the user or a formatter touched it, the edit fails with "re-read the file"). Writes are atomic (temp file + rename) so a crash never leaves half a file. After each edit, a PostToolUse hook or language server can run the formatter, linter or type checker and return diagnostics, so the model fixes its own errors in the next step. Every edit is checkpointed for /rewind. Whole-file Write remains for new files.

Challenges: many small edits mean more round trips; a common alternative is a "fast apply" step where the large model sketches the change and a small, fast model merges it into the file.

5) How do teams extend it without bloating every prompt?

The key question for every extension point is who decides when it runs, and when its text enters the context.

MechanismWho triggers itContext costUse for
CLAUDE.md / AGENTS.mdAlways loadedEvery callShort, always-relevant facts: commands, conventions
Slash commandsThe userOnly when invokedReusable prompts: /review, /release-notes
SkillsThe model, by matching the descriptionName + description always; body and files on demandProcedures and domain know-how loaded only when relevant
SubagentsThe model (or user) via AgentOnly the returned summaryIsolated work with its own prompt, tools and model
HooksLifecycle events (pre/post tool use, prompt submit, stop, session start, pre-compact)None unless they return outputDeterministic policy: format on save, block paths, notify
MCP serversThe model calls their toolsTool definitions (can be large)External systems: issue trackers, databases, browsers
PluginsInstalled by the user or orgWhatever they bundleDistributing all of the above as one package
Bad Solution
Put every instruction and tool into the system prompt

Challenges: context cost on every call, conflicting instructions, and "should" rules the model may ignore when the rule must hold every time.

Good Solution
Expose everything as MCP tools

Challenges: a few servers can add tens of thousands of tokens of tool definitions to every call, and tool choice degrades as the list grows. MCP servers are also third-party code with access to your context (supply-chain risk, Guardrails & Security).

Great Solution
Match the mechanism to the guarantee, and load lazily

Approach: anything that must happen goes in a hook (code, not a prompt). Always-relevant facts go in a short memory file. Procedures go in skills with progressive disclosure: only metadata sits in context until the task matches, then the body loads, then referenced files or scripts as needed (Anthropic, Agent Skills). Large tool catalogs are deferred behind a tool-search step so definitions load on demand. Isolated or parallel work goes to subagents with restricted tool lists. Organizations allowlist MCP servers and plugins through managed settings and pin versions.

Challenges: skill and subagent descriptions are the routing signal, so vague descriptions mean they never trigger; extension behavior needs the same evals as the core prompt.

6) How does it run in CI and in parallel?

Bad Solution
Run several agents in the same checkout, or the interactive tool in CI with permissions bypassed

Challenges: agents overwrite each other's files and fight over build outputs and ports; a bypassed agent in CI with repository secrets in the environment is a prompt-injection target with real credentials.

Good Solution
Headless mode with pre-declared permissions and separate clones

Approach: claude -p with an explicit allowed-tools list, a max-turns budget and JSON output, run per job; parallel work in separate clones.

Challenges: full clones are slow and disk-hungry for large repos.

Great Solution
One engine, three front ends, isolated workspaces

Approach: the loop is a library (Claude's Agent SDK), and the TUI, IDE extension and CLI -p are thin clients over its event stream. In CI it runs with least privilege: read-only token by default, scoped write token only for posting a comment or pushing a branch, network allowlist, turn and cost caps. Parallel sessions each get a git worktree (a separate working directory sharing one object store), their own ports and env, and background tasks for long-running dev servers whose output the agent polls. Work that should outlive the laptop is handed to a cloud runner (the cloud coding agent design).

Challenges: merging the results of parallel agents is still a human review problem; cost multiplies with parallelism.

7) How do we know a harness change made it better?

Bad Solution
Try a few prompts by hand

Challenges: agent runs are long and stochastic; a change to one tool description can help one task family and hurt another.

Good Solution
Public benchmarks

Approach: SWE-bench Verified (500 human-validated GitHub issues scored by hidden tests, OpenAI) and Terminal-Bench (tbench.ai) for terminal tasks.

Challenges: they measure model + harness on someone else's tasks, are at risk of contamination, and don't measure interactive qualities like asking good questions or respecting permissions.

Great Solution
A harness eval suite, A/B gates and privacy-respecting telemetry

Approach: build an internal suite of hundreds of tasks with verifiable outcomes (tests pass, the right file changed, no forbidden command ran), each in a container snapshot. Run every harness change (system prompt, tool descriptions, compaction prompt, defaults) and every new model across it several times and track pass rate, cost and tokens per solved task, turns, wall-clock, and permission prompts per task. Anthropic reports that refining tool descriptions measurably improved SWE-bench results, which is why tools get the same rigor as prompts (Writing effective tools). Online, track opt-in signals: interrupts, rewinds, "that's wrong" follow-ups, accepted versus reverted edits, session abandonment. See Evaluation.

Challenges: environment setup dominates the cost of the suite; flaky tasks must be quarantined or they drown real signal.

What is Expected at Each Level?

Mid-level

A clear agent loop with read, search, edit and shell tools; streaming output; a permission prompt before running commands; session transcripts. Mentions the context limit and truncating tool output when asked.

Senior

Distinguishes local harness from cloud agent; agentic search over embeddings with reasons; permission rules and modes plus an OS-level sandbox with network control; structured compaction and cache-friendly context ordering with cost math; reliable edit semantics with read-before-edit and checkpoints.

Staff+

Treats the harness as a platform: one engine behind TUI, IDE, CI and SDK; an extension model chosen by guarantee and context cost; enterprise policy and supply-chain controls for MCP and plugins; threat model built on the lethal trifecta; a harness eval suite and release gates for every prompt, tool and model change.

Question Breakdown · Hard

Design Copilot-style Code Autocomplete

Inline "ghost text" code suggestions that appear as a developer types, like GitHub Copilot completions or Cursor Tab. The LLM system design question where the latency budget is measured in hundreds of milliseconds.

Understanding the Problem

As a developer types in their editor, the tool predicts what comes next (the rest of the line, or the next few lines) and shows it as faint inline text. Tab accepts it; typing anything else dismisses it. Unlike chat or agents, nobody asked for this suggestion: it competes with the developer's own typing, so a suggestion that arrives late or is wrong is worse than none. That inverts the usual LLM trade-offs: small, fast models beat big, smart ones; latency is a correctness requirement; and the most important decision is often whether to show anything at all.

It is also a serving problem at enormous request volume. Cursor reports its Tab model handles over 400 million requests per day (Cursor, Improving Cursor Tab with online RL). Each request is small, but there are a lot of them, and most are thrown away before the user sees them.

Functional Requirements

  1. As a developer types, the editor should show inline suggestions (single-line or multi-line) at the cursor, which they can accept fully, accept word by word, or ignore by continuing to type.
  2. Suggestions should use context from the current file (code before and after the cursor) and from related files in the project.
  3. The system should be able to suggest the next edit elsewhere in the file, based on the edits the developer just made.
  4. Organization admins should be able to set policy: enable per org or repo, exclude files from ever being sent, and block suggestions that match public code.

Below the line: chat and agent modes (see Design Claude Code), pre-training the model, billing.

Non-Functional Requirements

  1. Latency: a suggestion visible within ~300 ms (p50) and ~600 ms (p95) of the developer pausing; after that the developer has usually typed on and the suggestion is stale. These are targets, not published figures; quantify them in your interview.
  2. Never block the editor: typing must stay fluid; under failure the system shows nothing rather than freezing or showing errors.
  3. Scale: ~2M daily active developers, ~1B requests/day, peaks around 3× average during working hours in each region.
  4. Quality: measured by acceptance rate and by characters accepted and retained in the code; showing fewer, better suggestions beats showing more.
  5. Privacy: code sent only as needed for the request; for business customers, prompts and suggestions are not retained or used for training; excluded files and secrets never leave the machine.
  6. Cost: completions are bundled into a per-seat price, so each request must cost a small fraction of a cent.

The Set Up

Core Entities

  • CompletionRequest: request id, document URI and language, cursor position, prefix, suffix, context snippets, editor state (single-line vs block position), client settings.
  • Suggestion: text, range to replace, model version, a confidence score, shown and accepted flags.
  • ContextSnippet: source (open tab, recent edit, symbol definition), file path, text, relevance score.
  • TelemetryEvent: shown, accepted (full or partial), rejected, and retained-after-N-seconds, keyed by request id, with no code by default.
  • OrgPolicy: enabled scopes, content exclusions, public-code filter, data retention setting.

API

POST /v1/completions     // HTTP/2, streamed; one in flight per editor
{ requestId, language, path,
  prefix, suffix,                       // code around the cursor (trimmed to budget)
  snippets: [{ path, text, source }],   // from open tabs, recent edits, symbols
  mode: "line" | "block", maxTokens }
→ stream of { textDelta } ... { done, finishReason, suggestionId }

// client cancels by resetting the HTTP/2 stream; the server must free the GPU slot
POST /v1/telemetry       { suggestionId, event: shown | accepted | partial | rejected | retained, chars }

Capacity estimate

2M developers × 500 requests/day      = 1B requests/day ≈ 11.6K req/s avg, ~35K peak
prompt ≈ 2K tokens, output ≈ 30 tokens (single line ~10, a block ~80)

prefill: 1B × 2K  = 2T tokens/day   ≈ 23M tokens/s
decode:  1B × 30  = 30B tokens/day  ≈ 350K tokens/s
→ input outweighs output ~70:1. This is a prefill-bound workload.

prefill compute for an assumed 7B-parameter model: 2 × 7e9 FLOP/token
  23M tok/s × 14 GFLOP = 3.2e17 FLOP/s
  H100 ≈ 989 TFLOP/s dense BF16; at ~50% utilization ≈ 0.5e15 FLOP/s
  → ~650 GPUs of prefill at average load with no caching (~3× at peak); ~130 if 80% of prompt tokens hit a prefix cache

The model size is an assumption for the math; the point is the shape. Consecutive requests from one developer share almost the whole prompt (the file changed by a few characters), so prefix caching with session-affine routing is the biggest cost lever, the same idea as in Caching for LLMs but at keystroke granularity.

High-Level Design

1) Showing suggestions as the developer types

Most of the latency budget is won or lost in the editor extension, before any network call:

  • Trigger rules: request after a short pause in typing, not on every keystroke; skip positions where completions are rarely accepted (middle of an identifier, inside a string literal in some languages) and decide line vs block mode from the cursor position (a block is only worth generating at the start of an empty function body or after a comment).
  • Debounce and cancel: each keystroke resets a timer of a few tens of milliseconds and cancels any in-flight request. Only one request per editor is ever live.
  • Typed-through cache: if the ghost text is return a + b and the developer types ret, keep showing urn a + b without a new request. A small LRU of recent (prompt hash → suggestion) entries also covers backspacing and undo.
  • Streaming render: show the first line as soon as it is complete; extend with later lines as they stream.

2) Gathering context

The model sees a fill-in-the-middle (FIM) prompt: the code before the cursor (prefix), the code after it (suffix), and sentinel tokens telling it to generate the middle (Bavarian et al., Efficient Training of Language Models to Fill in the Middle). Before FIM, Copilot only sent the prefix; GitHub reports FIM gave a 10% relative increase in accepted completions in A/B tests (GitHub blog).

Context from other files is added as commented snippets ahead of the prefix. GitHub's "neighboring tabs" technique uses files open in the editor and reported a 5% relative increase in acceptance (same post). A reverse-engineering analysis of an earlier Copilot client found it sliced each open file into fixed-size windows and picked the window with the highest Jaccard similarity (set overlap of tokens) to the code near the cursor (copilot-explorer; based on an older build, so treat the details as illustrative). The assembler fills a fixed token budget in priority order: prefix nearest the cursor, suffix, then retrieved snippets, dropping the lowest-value pieces first.

3) Serving the model

Requests go to the nearest region. An edge proxy authenticates, rate limits per user and applies org policy; a router sends each developer's requests to the same GPU replica so their prompt prefix is already in that replica's KV cache; the replica runs a small FIM model with continuous batching. Generation stops early on stop sequences and on structural signals (end of line in line mode; a dedent or closing bracket that ends the block in block mode). A post-processor trims text that duplicates the suffix (the model re-writing the closing brace that already exists) and balances brackets.

4) Org policy and next-edit suggestions

Policy is enforced twice: on the client (excluded paths are never read into a prompt) and at the edge (the server rejects requests for disabled repos). Before tokens leave the server, filters check for secrets and, if the org enabled it, for long matches against an index of public code. Next-edit suggestions reuse the same pipeline with a different prompt (recent edit history) and model, covered in deep dive 4.

Potential Deep Dives

1) How do we hit a ~300 ms budget?

One reasonable budget for a single-line suggestion after the developer pauses:

StageBudgetHow
Debounce~50 msShort timer; long enough to skip mid-burst keystrokes
Context gathering (client)≤ 20 msIncremental: snippet windows precomputed per open file, updated on edit
Network to regional edge20–60 msRegional serving; persistent HTTP/2 connection, no TLS handshake per request
Queue + prefill20–50 msSmall model; most of the prompt hits the prefix cache
Decode first line (~15 tokens)75–150 ms~100–200 tokens/s per stream on a small model
Post-process + render< 10 msShow the first line as soon as it's complete
Total≈ 200–340 ms
Bad Solution
A frontier chat model, called on every keystroke

Challenges: TTFT alone is often over a second; per-stream decode is slower; cost per request is orders of magnitude too high; and most requests are obsolete before they return.

Good Solution
Small FIM model, debounced requests, streaming, regional serving

Approach: a model trained for FIM on code, served close to users, with client-side debounce and streaming. GitHub reports its custom completions model delivered a 35% latency reduction and 3× token throughput over the previous one (GitHub blog).

Challenges: cancelled requests still burn GPU time if the server keeps generating; every request re-processes a 2K-token prompt from scratch.

Great Solution
Make cancellation real, make prefill nearly free, make decode speculative

Approach:

  • End-to-end cancellation: an HTTP/2 stream reset propagates through the proxy to the inference server, which evicts the sequence from the running batch at the next step. Requests whose deadline has passed are dropped from the queue instead of served.
  • Session-affine prefix caching: consistent hashing on user + file routes consecutive requests to the replica holding their KV cache. Prompt ordering matters: in the usual prefix-suffix-middle order, an edit at the cursor invalidates the cached suffix. The FIM paper's suffix-prefix-middle (SPM) variant puts the suffix first, so as the developer types, the prompt grows by appending and the cache keeps hitting.
  • Speculative decoding: code is repetitive, so drafting tokens by copying from the prompt (n-gram or "prompt lookup" drafting) or from a tiny draft model lets the main model verify several tokens per step. See Inference & Serving.
